# Model Evaluation, Validation, and Comparison

::: {.callout-note title="Connection with the theoretical volume"}
The mathematical treatment of confusion matrices, classification metrics, validation, and model selection is developed in greater depth in Chapters 6 and 7 of *Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning* [@rodriguez2026fundamentos].
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, the reader will be able to:

- explain why accuracy alone may be insufficient;
- construct and interpret a confusion matrix;
- compute accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1, and balanced accuracy;
- distinguish training, cross-validation, and final testing;
- select a classification threshold without using the test set;
- interpret ROC/AUC as measures of discrimination;
- distinguish discrimination from calibration;
- compare models using the same sample, split, and metrics;
- select models while considering performance, stability, interpretability, and error costs.

## Evaluation estimates generalization

Training a model is only one part of machine learning. The central question is:

> **How well will the model work on observations that were not used to build it?**

A model can fit training data extremely well and still fail on new observations. Reliable evaluation therefore protects the independence of the test set and uses metrics that match the practical goal of the problem [@kohavi1995crossvalidation; @james2021islr].

::: {.callout-important title="Separation principle"}
Any step that learns from data—imputation, scaling, feature selection, hyperparameter tuning, or threshold selection—must use training and validation information only. The final test set must not influence those decisions.
:::

## Load and prepare ATUS

```{r load-evaluation-atus-en}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
source("../util_graficas.R")

atus_path <- "../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv"

if (!file.exists(atus_path)) {
  stop("../datos/atus_ml_preparado.csv was not found. Run Chapter 2 first.")
}

atus_ml <- read_csv(atus_path, show_col_types = FALSE)

set.seed(2026)
atus_eval <- atus_ml |>
  mutate(
    accident_class = factor(
      accidente_con_victimas,
      levels = c("Solo daños", "Con víctimas"),
      labels = c("Property damage only", "With casualties")
    ),
    MES = factor(MES),
    HOUR_NUM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ID_HORA)),
    HOUR_NUM = ifelse(
      HOUR_NUM >= 0 & HOUR_NUM <= 23,
      HOUR_NUM,
      NA_real_
    ),
    DIASEMANA = factor(DIASEMANA),
    TIPACCID = factor(TIPACCID),
    CAUSAACCI = factor(CAUSAACCI)
  ) |>
  drop_na(
    accident_class,
    MES,
    HOUR_NUM,
    DIASEMANA,
    TIPACCID,
    CAUSAACCI
  ) |>
  slice_sample(n = min(15000, n()))

prop.table(table(atus_eval$accident_class))
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Class imbalance"}
When one class is much more frequent, high accuracy can be achieved by repeatedly predicting the majority class. Several metrics and a simple baseline are therefore required.
:::

## Confusion matrix

For the positive class **With casualties**:

| Actual class | Predicted positive | Predicted negative |
|---|---:|---:|
| Positive | TP | FN |
| Negative | FP | TN |

The principal metrics are

$$
Accuracy=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+FN+FP+TN},
$$

$$
Sensitivity=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},
\qquad
Specificity=\frac{TN}{TN+FP},
$$

$$
Precision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},
$$

$$
F_1=2\frac{Precision\cdot Sensitivity}{Precision+Sensitivity},
$$

and

$$
Balanced\ Accuracy=\frac{Sensitivity+Specificity}{2}.
$$

## Evaluation functions

```{r evaluation-functions-en}
classification_metrics <- function(actual, predicted, positive, negative) {
  actual <- factor(actual, levels = c(negative, positive))
  predicted <- factor(predicted, levels = c(negative, positive))
  m <- table(Actual = actual, Predicted = predicted)

  TP <- m[positive, positive]
  FN <- m[positive, negative]
  FP <- m[negative, positive]
  TN <- m[negative, negative]

  safe_divide <- function(a, b) if (b == 0) NA_real_ else as.numeric(a / b)

  sensitivity <- safe_divide(TP, TP + FN)
  specificity <- safe_divide(TN, TN + FP)
  precision <- safe_divide(TP, TP + FP)
  f1 <- if (
    is.na(precision) || is.na(sensitivity) ||
    precision + sensitivity == 0
  ) {
    NA_real_
  } else {
    2 * precision * sensitivity / (precision + sensitivity)
  }

  list(
    confusion = m,
    metrics = data.frame(
      accuracy = safe_divide(TP + TN, sum(m)),
      sensitivity = sensitivity,
      specificity = specificity,
      precision = precision,
      f1 = f1,
      balanced_accuracy = mean(c(sensitivity, specificity), na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  )
}

auc_by_ranks <- function(y_binary, probability) {
  n1 <- sum(y_binary == 1)
  n0 <- sum(y_binary == 0)
  if (n1 == 0 || n0 == 0) return(NA_real_)

  ranks <- rank(probability, ties.method = "average")
  (sum(ranks[y_binary == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
```

## Stratified training-test split

Eighty percent of the data are used for model development and 20% remain untouched until final evaluation.

```{r evaluation-split-atus-en}
set.seed(2026)

idx_train <- unlist(
  lapply(
    split(seq_len(nrow(atus_eval)), atus_eval$accident_class),
    function(ids) sample(ids, floor(0.80 * length(ids)))
  )
)

idx_train <- sort(idx_train)
train <- atus_eval[idx_train, ]
test <- atus_eval[-idx_train, ]

rbind(
  training = prop.table(table(train$accident_class)),
  test = prop.table(table(test$accident_class))
)
```

## Majority-class baseline

```{r evaluation-baseline-en}
majority_class <- names(which.max(table(train$accident_class)))

pred_baseline <- factor(
  rep(majority_class, nrow(test)),
  levels = levels(train$accident_class)
)

result_baseline <- classification_metrics(
  test$accident_class,
  pred_baseline,
  positive = "With casualties",
  negative = "Property damage only"
)

result_baseline$confusion
result_baseline$metrics
```

::: {.callout-warning title="A baseline is essential"}
A complex model should outperform or otherwise justify itself against a simple rule. Under strong imbalance, the majority baseline can have surprisingly high accuracy while having zero sensitivity for the minority class.
:::

# Threshold selection without touching the test set

## Create stratified folds inside training data

```{r create-evaluation-folds-en}
create_folds <- function(response, k = 5, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  response <- factor(response)
  folds <- integer(length(response))

  for (class_value in levels(response)) {
    ids <- which(response == class_value)
    labels <- rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(ids))
    folds[ids] <- sample(labels)
  }

  folds
}

fold <- create_folds(
  train$accident_class,
  k = 5,
  seed = 2026
)

table(fold, train$accident_class)
```

## Generate out-of-fold probabilities

Each training observation receives a probability from a model that **was not fitted using that observation**.

```{r logistic-oof-probabilities-en}
prob_oof <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(train))

for (k in 1:5) {
  cv_train <- train[fold != k, ]
  cv_validation <- train[fold == k, ]

  model_cv <- glm(
    accident_class ~
      MES + HOUR_NUM + DIASEMANA + TIPACCID + CAUSAACCI,
    data = cv_train,
    family = binomial
  )

  prob_oof[fold == k] <- predict(
    model_cv,
    newdata = cv_validation,
    type = "response"
  )
}

summary(prob_oof)
```

Because **With casualties** is the second factor level, `glm()` models its probability.

## Choose the threshold using balanced accuracy

```{r select-threshold-oof-en}
thresholds <- seq(0.10, 0.90, by = 0.05)

threshold_metrics <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(thresholds, function(threshold) {
    pred <- factor(
      ifelse(
        prob_oof >= threshold,
        "With casualties",
        "Property damage only"
      ),
      levels = c("Property damage only", "With casualties")
    )

    m <- classification_metrics(
      train$accident_class,
      pred,
      positive = "With casualties",
      negative = "Property damage only"
    )$metrics

    cbind(threshold = threshold, m)
  })
)

threshold_metrics

best_threshold <- threshold_metrics$threshold[
  which.max(threshold_metrics$balanced_accuracy)
]

best_threshold
```

```{r threshold-plot-oof-en, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.8}
threshold_long <- threshold_metrics |>
  select(threshold, sensitivity, specificity, balanced_accuracy, f1) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -threshold,
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(
  threshold_long,
  aes(x = threshold, y = value, color = metric)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.05) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = best_threshold, linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Threshold selection with out-of-fold predictions",
    subtitle = "The final test set does not participate in this decision",
    x = "Threshold",
    y = "Metric",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-note title="The criterion depends on the problem"}
Balanced accuracy is used here to give equal weight to sensitivity and specificity. Other applications may prioritize sensitivity, precision, expected cost, or a utility function defined with domain experts.
:::

# Discrimination: ROC and AUC

The ROC curve plots sensitivity against false-positive rate over many thresholds. AUC summarizes how well the model ranks positive observations above negative observations [@fawcett2006roc].

```{r auc-oof-evaluation-en}
y_oof <- ifelse(train$accident_class == "With casualties", 1, 0)
auc_oof <- auc_by_ranks(y_oof, prob_oof)
auc_oof
```

```{r roc-oof-en, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=5}
roc_thresholds <- sort(unique(c(0, prob_oof, 1)), decreasing = TRUE)

roc_oof <- do.call(
  rbind,
  lapply(roc_thresholds, function(u) {
    pred_binary <- ifelse(prob_oof >= u, 1, 0)
    TP <- sum(pred_binary == 1 & y_oof == 1)
    FN <- sum(pred_binary == 0 & y_oof == 1)
    FP <- sum(pred_binary == 1 & y_oof == 0)
    TN <- sum(pred_binary == 0 & y_oof == 0)

    data.frame(
      fpr = ifelse(FP + TN == 0, NA, FP / (FP + TN)),
      tpr = ifelse(TP + FN == 0, NA, TP / (TP + FN))
    )
  })
)

ggplot(roc_oof, aes(x = fpr, y = tpr)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 1.1, color = col_azul) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Out-of-fold ROC; AUC = ", round(auc_oof, 3)),
    x = "False-positive rate",
    y = "Sensitivity"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-warning title="AUC is not calibration"}
AUC measures discrimination or ranking ability. A model can have a useful AUC and still produce probabilities that are systematically too high or too low.
:::

# Final fit and one-time test evaluation

```{r final-evaluation-model-en}
final_logistic <- glm(
  accident_class ~
    MES + HOUR_NUM + DIASEMANA + TIPACCID + CAUSAACCI,
  data = train,
  family = binomial
)

prob_test <- predict(
  final_logistic,
  newdata = test,
  type = "response"
)

pred_test <- factor(
  ifelse(
    prob_test >= best_threshold,
    "With casualties",
    "Property damage only"
  ),
  levels = c("Property damage only", "With casualties")
)

result_logistic <- classification_metrics(
  test$accident_class,
  pred_test,
  positive = "With casualties",
  negative = "Property damage only"
)

result_logistic$confusion
result_logistic$metrics
```

## Final test AUC

```{r auc-test-evaluation-en}
y_test_binary <- ifelse(test$accident_class == "With casualties", 1, 0)
auc_test <- auc_by_ranks(y_test_binary, prob_test)
auc_test
```

## Calibration on the test set

```{r calibration-test-evaluation-en}
calibration_test <- data.frame(
  probability = prob_test,
  actual = y_test_binary
) |>
  mutate(group = ntile(probability, 10)) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_probability = mean(probability),
    observed_frequency = mean(actual),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

calibration_test
```

```{r calibration-plot-test-en, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=5}
ggplot(
  calibration_test,
  aes(x = mean_probability, y = observed_frequency)
) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Calibration on the final test set",
    x = "Mean predicted probability",
    y = "Observed frequency"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Calibration also depends on sampling"}
Probabilities retain a population interpretation only when the sampling process and prevalence permit it, or when appropriate weighting and calibration corrections are applied.
:::

## Compare with the baseline

```{r compare-baseline-logistic-en}
comparison_atus <- bind_rows(
  cbind(model = "Majority baseline", result_baseline$metrics),
  cbind(model = "Logistic regression", result_logistic$metrics)
)

comparison_atus
```

```{r evaluation-comparison-plot-en, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.8}
comparison_long <- comparison_atus |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -model,
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(
  comparison_long,
  aes(x = metric, y = value, fill = model)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Final comparison with a simple baseline",
    x = "Metric",
    y = "Value",
    fill = "Model"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

**Source:** Author's processing of INEGI ATUS 2024 data [@inegi_atus_2024].

# Common educational benchmark with COVID-19

Up to this point, the book has introduced logistic regression, k-NN, decision trees, and Random Forest. We compare them using **the same sample, predictors, and test split**. SVM, Naive Bayes, and neural networks will be added to the integrated comparison after their own chapters have been developed.

::: {.callout-important title="Educational benchmark, not clinical evaluation"}
A balanced class sample is constructed to facilitate algorithm comparison. The resulting metrics describe this benchmark and do not represent mortality prevalence or population risk.
:::

## Select the period and create a balanced sample

```{r covid-benchmark-prepare-en}
covid_counts <- read_csv(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados/conteo_casos_confirmados_2020_2025.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

covid_year <- covid_counts |>
  filter(ESTADO == "PROCESADO", !is.na(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS)) |>
  slice_max(CASOS_CONFIRMADOS, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  pull(ANIO)

covid_path <- file.path(
  "../datos/covid19/procesados",
  paste0("covid19_mexico_", covid_year, "_ml_preparado.csv.gz")
)

covid_base <- read_csv(covid_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(
    MURIO, EDAD, NEUMONIA, DIABETES, HIPERTENSION,
    OBESIDAD, RENAL_CRONICA, NUM_COMORBILIDADES
  ) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    outcome = factor(
      MURIO,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("No recorded death", "Recorded death")
    )
  ) |>
  select(-MURIO)

set.seed(2026)
n_per_class <- min(2000, min(table(covid_base$outcome)))

covid_benchmark <- covid_base |>
  group_by(outcome) |>
  slice_sample(n = n_per_class) |>
  ungroup()
```

## Common 80/20 split

```{r covid-benchmark-split-en}
set.seed(2026)

idx_covid_train <- unlist(
  lapply(
    split(seq_len(nrow(covid_benchmark)), covid_benchmark$outcome),
    function(ids) sample(ids, floor(0.80 * length(ids)))
  )
)

train_comp <- covid_benchmark[sort(idx_covid_train), ]
test_comp <- covid_benchmark[-sort(idx_covid_train), ]

prop.table(table(train_comp$outcome))
prop.table(table(test_comp$outcome))
```

## Common metric function

```{r covid-benchmark-metric-en}
covid_metrics <- function(actual, predicted) {
  classification_metrics(
    actual,
    predicted,
    positive = "Recorded death",
    negative = "No recorded death"
  )$metrics
}
```

## 1. Logistic regression

```{r covid-benchmark-logistic-en}
model_log_comp <- glm(
  outcome ~ EDAD + NEUMONIA + DIABETES + HIPERTENSION +
    OBESIDAD + RENAL_CRONICA + NUM_COMORBILIDADES,
  data = train_comp,
  family = binomial
)

prob_log_comp <- predict(model_log_comp, test_comp, type = "response")
pred_log_comp <- factor(
  ifelse(prob_log_comp >= 0.50, "Recorded death", "No recorded death"),
  levels = levels(train_comp$outcome)
)
```

## 2. k-NN

For this benchmark, $k=11$ is fixed **before inspecting the test results**. The purpose is a common didactic comparison rather than exhaustive hyperparameter optimization.

```{r covid-benchmark-knn-en}
vars_comp <- c(
  "EDAD", "NEUMONIA", "DIABETES", "HIPERTENSION",
  "OBESIDAD", "RENAL_CRONICA", "NUM_COMORBILIDADES"
)

X_train <- as.matrix(train_comp[vars_comp])
X_test <- as.matrix(test_comp[vars_comp])

X_train_z <- X_train
X_test_z <- X_test

for (variable in c("EDAD", "NUM_COMORBILIDADES")) {
  mean_value <- mean(X_train[, variable])
  sd_value <- sd(X_train[, variable])
  if (sd_value == 0) sd_value <- 1

  X_train_z[, variable] <- (X_train[, variable] - mean_value) / sd_value
  X_test_z[, variable] <- (X_test[, variable] - mean_value) / sd_value
}

pred_knn_comp <- class::knn(
  train = X_train_z,
  test = X_test_z,
  cl = train_comp$outcome,
  k = 11
)
```

## 3. Decision tree

Complexity is selected using internal cross-validation in the training data.

```{r covid-benchmark-tree-en}
large_tree_comp <- rpart::rpart(
  outcome ~ EDAD + NEUMONIA + DIABETES + HIPERTENSION +
    OBESIDAD + RENAL_CRONICA + NUM_COMORBILIDADES,
  data = train_comp,
  method = "class",
  control = rpart::rpart.control(
    cp = 0.0005,
    minsplit = 60,
    minbucket = 20,
    maxdepth = 8,
    xval = 5
  )
)

cp_comp <- large_tree_comp$cptable[
  which.min(large_tree_comp$cptable[, "xerror"]),
  "CP"
]

model_tree_comp <- rpart::prune(large_tree_comp, cp = cp_comp)
pred_tree_comp <- predict(model_tree_comp, test_comp, type = "class")
```

## 4. Random Forest

`mtry = 3` is fixed before final evaluation to keep the benchmark lightweight and reproducible.

```{r covid-benchmark-rf-en}
set.seed(2026)

model_rf_comp <- ranger::ranger(
  outcome ~ EDAD + NEUMONIA + DIABETES + HIPERTENSION +
    OBESIDAD + RENAL_CRONICA + NUM_COMORBILIDADES,
  data = train_comp,
  num.trees = 250,
  mtry = 3,
  min.node.size = 20,
  probability = FALSE,
  seed = 2026
)

pred_rf_comp <- predict(model_rf_comp, test_comp)$predictions
```

## Comparison table

```{r covid-benchmark-table-en}
comparison_covid <- bind_rows(
  cbind(model = "Logistic regression", covid_metrics(test_comp$outcome, pred_log_comp)),
  cbind(model = "k-NN (k=11)", covid_metrics(test_comp$outcome, pred_knn_comp)),
  cbind(model = "Decision tree", covid_metrics(test_comp$outcome, pred_tree_comp)),
  cbind(model = "Random Forest", covid_metrics(test_comp$outcome, pred_rf_comp))
)

comparison_covid |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

```{r covid-benchmark-plot-en, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
comparison_covid_long <- comparison_covid |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -model,
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  )

ggplot(
  comparison_covid_long,
  aes(x = model, y = value, fill = metric)
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Common COVID-19 benchmark",
    subtitle = "Same balanced sample and same final test split",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Metric value",
    fill = "Metric"
  ) +
  tema_libro()
```

::: {.callout-important title="There is no universal winner"}
The best choice depends on error costs, stability, interpretability, computational cost, and whether calibrated probabilities are required. A small difference in accuracy does not automatically justify a much more complex model.
:::

# Interactive laboratory: confusion matrix metrics

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}
Change TP, TN, FP, and FN and observe how the classification metrics respond.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 720
#| components: [viewer]

library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Classification metrics calculator"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      numericInput("tp", "True positives", 40, min = 0),
      numericInput("tn", "True negatives", 45, min = 0),
      numericInput("fp", "False positives", 5, min = 0),
      numericInput("fn", "False negatives", 10, min = 0)
    ),
    mainPanel(
      tableOutput("matrix"),
      tableOutput("metrics"),
      plotOutput("plot", height = "320px")
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  calc <- reactive({
    tp <- input$tp; tn <- input$tn; fp <- input$fp; fn <- input$fn
    total <- tp + tn + fp + fn
    accuracy <- ifelse(total == 0, NA, (tp + tn) / total)
    sensitivity <- ifelse(tp + fn == 0, NA, tp / (tp + fn))
    specificity <- ifelse(tn + fp == 0, NA, tn / (tn + fp))
    precision <- ifelse(tp + fp == 0, NA, tp / (tp + fp))
    f1 <- ifelse(
      is.na(precision) || is.na(sensitivity) || precision + sensitivity == 0,
      NA,
      2 * precision * sensitivity / (precision + sensitivity)
    )
    balanced <- mean(c(sensitivity, specificity), na.rm = TRUE)

    list(
      matrix = matrix(
        c(tn, fp, fn, tp),
        nrow = 2,
        byrow = TRUE,
        dimnames = list(
          "Actual" = c("Class 0", "Class 1"),
          "Predicted" = c("Class 0", "Class 1")
        )
      ),
      metrics = c(
        Accuracy = accuracy,
        Sensitivity = sensitivity,
        Specificity = specificity,
        Precision = precision,
        F1 = f1,
        Balanced_accuracy = balanced
      )
    )
  })

  output$matrix <- renderTable({
    as.data.frame.matrix(calc()$matrix)
  }, rownames = TRUE)

  output$metrics <- renderTable({
    data.frame(
      Metric = names(calc()$metrics),
      Value = round(as.numeric(calc()$metrics), 4)
    )
  })

  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    m <- calc()$metrics
    barplot(
      m,
      ylim = c(0, 1),
      ylab = "Value",
      main = "Model metrics"
    )
    abline(h = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2), lty = 3)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```
:::

## Activities for the reader

1. Change the threshold-selection objective: maximize sensitivity subject to specificity of at least 0.70.
2. Compare AUC with balanced accuracy and explain why they answer different questions.
3. Repeat the COVID-19 benchmark while preserving natural class imbalance and compare the conclusions.
4. Add SVM, Naive Bayes, and neural networks after studying those chapters.
5. Write a technical recommendation of no more than 200 words justifying a model choice.

## Chapter summary

Professional evaluation clearly separates **model development** from **final testing**. Hyperparameters and thresholds are chosen without looking at the test set; AUC evaluates discrimination, calibration evaluates probabilities, and threshold-dependent metrics quantify specific error types. Fair model comparison requires the same sample, split, and criteria. There is no universally best model: the appropriate choice depends on the objective and the consequences of error.

## Fundamental references

Cross-validation was comparatively studied by @kohavi1995crossvalidation. A widely used reference for ROC curves and AUC is @fawcett2006roc. An integrated treatment of data splitting, resampling, and model comparison appears in @james2021islr.
